column2: After Joshua's death Israel inquires of the Lord about who will lead battle against the Canaanites; the selected leading participle is represented without adding first.
Judah shall ascend, and Behold introduces the completed divine gift into his hand; the singular tribal personification remains.
Judah invites brother Simeon into his own allotted territory and promises reciprocal help; I also represents the selected emphasis, and Simeon's actual departure remains.
Judah ascends, the Lord gives both peoples into his hand and he strikes ten thousand at Bezek; singular action follows the collective tribal name.
Plural they find Adoni-bezek, fight him and strike Canaanites and Perizzites; the shift from the preceding singular Judah remains.
Flight, pursuit, seizure and cutting off hand/foot extremities remain. Extremities preserves akra without specifying thumbs and great toes not named in this selected line.
Seventy mutilated kings gathered beneath the table; Adoni-bezek interprets his fate as divine repayment before being brought to Jerusalem and dying there.
Judah's sons capture Jerusalem, strike with the sword's edge and burn it with fire; no harmonization with the later Jebusite residence notice is imposed.
The subsequent descent targets Canaanites in hill country, south and plain, preserving all three regions.
Hebron itself comes out against Judah; the selected combined Kariatharboksepher and Sheshai/Ahiman/Talmai as Anak's descendants remain.
column3: The combined former name is not divided or harmonized to Joshua's shorter Arbok notice; its textual history remains uncollated.

column2: Plural they go to Debir, whose former name is translated City of Letters; the selected naming statement remains.
Caleb offers Achsah to whoever strikes and takes possession of the City of Letters; both actions precede the marriage promise.
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, takes possession; explicit Caleb in the English giving clause supplies the contextual antecedent of the source's implicit subject.
column3: The younger-brother apposition is nominative in Greek and favors Othniel; English kinship attachment remains potentially ambiguous, as in Joshua 15:17.

column2: He urges Achsah to ask for the field; she murmurs and cries from the beast, repeating the southern-land complaint before Caleb's question. This differs from Joshua's selected dialogue and is retained.
column3: The unstated urging subject is contextually Othniel; what do you desire interprets what is with you as a request inquiry, not a separate desire verb.

column2: The repeated southern-land complaint, redemption of water, according to her heart, and redemptions of heights and low places remain. Give represents the future dōseis as a request in context.
column3: Lytrosis is opaque here; no familiar springs reading is substituted. Both its lexical sense and whether the future should be more explicitly represented remain specialist questions.

column2: Jobab the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, his descendants, City of Palms, southern wilderness and Arad descent remain; singular he went/dwelt follows the plural opening.
column3: The singular final actor is not named, and Jobab is not silently changed to a familiar father-in-law name.

column2: Judah and Simeon strike Sepheth, place it under the ban, destroy it and name it Destruction; the ban and destruction actions remain distinct.
The selected negative conquest notice includes Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron and Ashdod, with territory for the first three and surrounding lands for Ashdod.
The Lord with Judah, mountain inheritance, inability regarding valley inhabitants and Rechab's separation remain with both because clauses.
column3: Rechab and the difficult inherited inherit the inhabitants wording remain unresolved; neither iron chariots nor a changed causal sequence is imported.

column2: Hebron is given to Caleb according to Moses' word, followed by the selected three cities and removal of Anak's three sons.
column3: The first giver is implicit; the later English Caleb supplies the contextual inheritor, without resolving whether the first he refers to Judah or the Lord.

column2: Benjamin fails to remove Jerusalem's Jebusites, who remain with Benjamin to this day; neither the tribe nor the time expression is harmonized to Joshua 15:63.
Joseph's sons also ascend to Bethel and Judah is with them; the selected Judah is not replaced with the Lord.
The house of Israel camps against Bethel, formerly Luz; Israel is retained rather than silently changed to Joseph to match the preceding line.
The watchers see and seize the departing man, request the entrance and promise mercy; seizure and the promise both remain.
The shown entrance leads to the city's sword-striking, while the man and his kin are released; the contrasting treatment is retained.
The released man builds and names Luz in the Hittite land, and the name persists to this day; this second Luz is not merged with the former city's identity.

The full selected list includes Beth-shan/City of the Scythians, Ekthanaad, Dor, Balaam, Magedon and Jeblaam, with dependent-town clauses and Beth-shan's surrounding lands. Canaanites begin to dwell there.
column3: Dependent towns interprets daughters as satellite settlements; Balaam and Jeblaam remain separate entries, without reconstruction of the list.

column2: Israel's strength leads to tribute but not complete removal; the emphatic repeated removal construction is represented by completely.
Ephraim's failure at Gezer, Canaanite residence among them and tribute remain; the collective singular tribe and people are naturally pluralized in the residence clause.
Zebulun fails at Kedron and Enaala; residence and tribute follow, preserving both selected places.
Asher's failure at Acco includes an immediate tribute clause before Dor, Sidon, Aalaph, Achazib, Helba, Aphek and Roob; the longer selected list remains.
Asher lives among the Canaanites because he cannot remove them; the subject is Asher, not the Canaanites.
Naphtali fails at Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath, but Israel is the named resident among Canaanites. Both towns become tributary; Israel is not silently changed to Naphtali.
Amorite pressure confines Dan to the mountain and prevents descent to the valley; the collective parties are retained without changing agency.
The Amorites begin residence on the Mountain of the Myrtle Grove, where bears and foxes are, before Joseph's heavy hand and tribute; the selected animal clause remains.
column3: Myrsinōn is rendered as the grove expression in the inherited title; no alternate mountain or city sequence is substituted.

column2: The Amorite boundary, the Idumean expression, above Akrabin, Rock and above remain in the inherited elliptical formulation.
column3: The apposition and geographic relation are unresolved; the punctuation is provisional and no smooth reconstruction is claimed.

column2: The messenger's route includes Gilgal, Place of Weeping, Bethel and Israel's house. Repeated Lord, Lord and the transition from third-person report to quoted I will never scatter My covenant remain.
column3: Scatter preserves diaskedannymi but its covenant sense needs lexical review; messenger identity and quotation framing are not treated as settled theology.

column2: No covenant with inhabitants, no bowing to their gods, breaking images and demolishing altars precede the failure to obey My voice when these things were done.
column3: The inherited inner-quotation break before Yet leaves first-person divine speech within the messenger's words; the scope of these things remains open.

column2: The announced cessation of removal retains the people previously marked for destruction, constraints upon Israel and their gods as a stumbling block.
column3: Constraints is a working rendering of synochai; no thorns image from a different text is substituted.

column2: All Israel hears the messenger, raises its voice and weeps; the collective voice and plural weeping action remain.
The place receives its Weeping name because of the event, and sacrifice to the Lord occurs there; the explanation and action remain distinct.
Joshua dismisses the people, each to house and inheritance to possess the land; this retrospective sequence is not moved to harmonize chronology.
Service spans Joshua and the elders who outlive him and know the Lord's great work; knowing remains distinct from seeing in Joshua 24:29.
Joshua son of Nun, the Lord's servant, dies aged one hundred ten; the age idiom is represented as age, not a literal son construction.
Burial within his inheritance retains Timnath-heres, Ephraim's mountain and north of Gaash; the selected place form is not harmonized to Joshua's burial spelling.
The whole generation is added to its fathers, and another arises without knowing the Lord or His work for Israel; the inherited gathered-to-fathers image remains.
Israel does evil before the Lord and serves the Baalim; the plural divine-name form is retained.
Forsaking the ancestral God who brought them from Egypt leads to following surrounding peoples' gods, bowing and provoking the Lord; all actions remain.
The repeated forsaking notice names Baal and plural Astartes, distinct from the preceding Baalim form.
Divine anger, handing to plunderers, actual plundering, selling to surrounding enemies and inability to withstand them remain; the exchange metaphor is preserved.
The selected prostitution expression frames the Lord's hand for harm, as spoken and sworn, and His great affliction; it is not replaced with a generic wherever they went.
The Lord raises judges and saves Israel from plunderers; the saving verb retains the Lord's agency rather than assigning it solely to the judges.
Even the judges are not heard; prostitution, bowing, provocation and quick departure from the fathers' obedient way remain. The final as their fathers had done makes the antecedent of thus explicit.
Whenever judges arise, the Lord accompanies the judge and saves throughout his days, moved by groaning under besiegers and abusers.
column3: Moved for pareklēthē is provisional; comforted, entreated and relenting senses need contextual lexical review, as do related occurrences later in Judges.

column2: The judge's death brings return and explicit again, increased corruption over the fathers, other-god service and refusal to abandon practices or the hard way.
The Lord's anger introduces the causal covenant accusation against this nation and its failure to hear His voice; the sentence continues into the next unit.
I too will no longer remove anyone from the remaining nations preserves the single-man negative scope and Joshua's double leaving expression.
The purpose is testing whether Israel keeps and walks the Lord's way as the fathers did, or not; the explicit alternative and purpose remain.
column3: The inherited quotation closes before this purpose statement although Greek does not supply modern quotation marks; speech/narration boundary remains editorial.

column2: The Lord leaves the nations without rapid removal and without handing them to Joshua; the negative purpose/result and final negative grant remain.
The selected subject leaving the nations is Joshua. Testing includes those unacquainted with Canaan's wars; no Lord substitution is made.
The two restrictive plēn expressions, generations, teaching warfare and the earlier group's lack of knowledge remain in the inherited difficult sequence.
column3: The relation of those before them to the generations is obscure; no rewriting to the familiar those who had not previously known war is claimed.

column2: Five foreign satrapies, all Canaanites, Sidonians and Lebanon's Hivites from Balaermon to Loboemath remain; the geographical endpoints are not normalized.
Testing aims to know obedience to the Lord's commands given the fathers through Moses; purpose and the paternal audience remain.
Israel resides among six listed peoples in order: Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites; no seventh group is added.
Reciprocal daughter exchanges lead to service of the other peoples' gods; own daughters clarifies the switch of possessive antecedent within the repeated their wording.
Evil, forgetting the Lord and service of Baalim and groves remain; the selected groves expression is not silently replaced by a reconstructed cult object.
The Lord sells Israel into Chousarsathom's hands, king of Syria of the Rivers, for eight years; selected name, regional title and duration remain.
Israel cries, the Lord raises Othniel as saviour and saves them, then he heard him remains without supplying named referents to the final pair.
column3: The final subject/object antecedents and the younger-brother attachment remain open; the text is not rewritten as an unambiguous prayer response.

column2: The Lord's Spirit comes upon Othniel, who judges and wars; divine handing over and his strengthened hand against Chousarsathom remain separate actions.
The selected quiet period is fifty years before Othniel's death; it is not replaced with forty.
Israel again does evil and the Lord strengthens Eglon because of that evil; divine agency, recurrence and causation remain.
The implicit he gathers all Ammon and Amalek, strikes Israel and possesses the City of Palms; the working antecedent is Eglon.
column3: The subject is not restated in Greek after the Lord's strengthening action; the narrative antecedent should remain visible as an interpretive choice.

column2: Israel serves Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years; the figure agrees with the selected Joshua ending, without requiring name normalization.
Ehud's genealogy includes Gera and Jemeni, his skill is both-handed, and Israel sends gifts through him; no left-handed limitation or reconstructed tribal label is substituted.
The double-edged dagger is a span long beneath his cloak on the right thigh; the selected measure and side remain.
Eglon is very handsome for asteios; the later fat detail does not authorize replacing this selected adjective with fat here.
After Ehud finishes presenting gifts he dismisses their bearers; the sequence and identity of the dismissed people remain.
Eglon is explicitly the returning subject near Gilgal's images; Ehud then offers a secret word and Eglon dismisses all attendants. No switch of the first subject to Ehud is made.
Ehud enters the king's summer upper room, where the king is all alone, and announces God's word; Eglon rises near him from the throne.
As the king rises, Ehud uses his left hand to draw from his right thigh and strike the belly; timing and both sides remain.
Even the handle follows the blade, fat closes over it, and the dagger is not withdrawn; no additional bodily-discharge clause is imported.
Ehud exits into the vestibule, closes the upper-room doors upon the king and fastens them; no new agent or exit route is supplied.
The repeated exit remains. Restore the explicit idou discovery with and behold after the attendants enter and look; the selected possible privy use in the bedroom retreat remains as their question.
column3: The room/retreat terminology remains a working architectural and idiomatic interpretation; no independent specialist review is claimed.

column2: Restore the first idou with and behold before no one opens, replacing simple but. The final there was their lord remains a natural presentative for the second idou; the fallen-dead posture and key opening are unchanged.
Ehud escapes during their confusion and inattention, passes the images and escapes to Seirotha; both escape verbs and the no-one attention clause remain.
Arrival leads to sounding a horn in Ephraim's mountain, Israel's descent with him and his position before them; no additional summons is inserted.
The descent command rests on the Lord God's handing over Moab; seizure of Jordan crossings and allowing no man through remain.
About ten thousand Moabites, all fighters and every man of strength, are struck with no escape; the approximate number and inclusive descriptions remain.
Moab is put to shame under Israel's hand, the land rests eighty years and Ehud judges until death; the selected final judging clause remains.
Shamgar son of Anath strikes up to six hundred foreign men, apart from the calves of the oxen, and saves Israel; the opaque selected animal phrase remains.
column3: The inherited dagger question about ektos moschōn tōn boōn remains unresolved; no oxgoad reading or invented weapon is substituted.
